method_card.title: How to read orchestral scores: clefs, transpositions and instrument identification
method_card.content:
A full orchestral score contains multiple staves — one (or more) per instrument. This lesson teaches you to navigate an orchestral score and identify instruments from their stave position, clef, and transposition.

Clefs:

  • Treble clef: G clef — G is on the second line. Used by violin, flute, oboe, clarinet, trumpet, horn.
  • Bass clef: F clef — F is on the fourth line. Used by cello, double bass, bassoon, trombone, left-hand piano.
  • Alto clef: C clef on the middle line — middle C is on the third line. Used by the viola.
  • Tenor clef: C clef on the fourth line. Used by upper cello, upper bassoon passages.

Score order (top to bottom in a Classical orchestra score):

  1. Woodwind: flutes, oboes, clarinets, bassoons
  2. Brass: horns, trumpets, (trombones, tuba in later works)
  3. Percussion: timpani
  4. Strings: first violins, second violins, violas, cellos, double basses

Transposing instruments:

  • Clarinet in B♭: written a tone higher than it sounds. Written C = sounds B♭.
  • Clarinet in A: written a minor third higher. Written C = sounds A.
  • Horn in F: written a perfect fifth higher than it sounds. Written C = sounds F.
steps: Find the clef at the start of each staff: treble (G), bass (F), alto/tenor (C).
Check the score order: woodwind on top, brass in the middle, strings at the bottom.
For transposing instruments, look for a different key signature or transposition label at the start.
Identify the instrument family of a mystery line by its clef position and range.

bronze.question: Look at Excerpt C (Chopin Nocturne piano score). What clef does the right hand (melody) use?
bronze.explanation: The right hand of a piano score uses the treble (G) clef. The melody sits in the upper staff with the treble clef. The left hand uses the bass (F) clef. Together the two staves joined by a brace form the piano 'grand staff'.

bronze.question: In a Classical orchestra score, which section of the orchestra is written at the top of the score?
bronze.explanation: The standard Western orchestral score order from top to bottom is: woodwind, brass, percussion, strings. Woodwind (flutes, oboes, clarinets, bassoons) always occupy the top staves.

bronze.question: Match each clef name to the instrument(s) that typically use it.

pairs.right: Cello, double bass, bassoon, left-hand piano

bronze.explanation: Clef knowledge is directly tested in the AQA listening exam. The viola is the only orchestral string that routinely uses the alto clef. The piano grand staff always uses treble (right hand) and bass (left hand) clefs together.

silver.question: In a Classical orchestra, the clarinet in B♭ is a transposing instrument. If a clarinet in B♭ reads a written C, what pitch does it sound?
silver.explanation: The clarinet in B♭ transposes down a tone: the written note sounds a major second lower than written. So a written C sounds B♭. This is why the clarinet part has a different key signature from the rest of the orchestra — the part is written a tone higher so the player reads normal fingerings.

silver.question: Which instrument in the orchestra uses the alto clef (C clef on the middle line)?
silver.explanation: The viola is the only standard orchestral instrument that routinely uses the alto clef. The alto clef places middle C on the middle line of the staff. Violas read this clef because their range sits between the violin (treble clef) and cello (bass clef). Spotting an alto clef in an exam score means you're looking at the viola line.

silver.question: Put these orchestral instrument families in the correct score order from top (highest stave) to bottom (lowest stave) in a Classical orchestra score.
silver.explanation: The standard Classical orchestra score order from top to bottom is: woodwind → brass → percussion → strings. Strings always occupy the bottom staves. This ordering is followed consistently in all Classical and Romantic orchestral scores.

gold.question: Mozart's Symphony No.40 uses clarinets in B♭ (in the revised 1791 version). In the score, the clarinet part has a different key signature from the strings. If the strings are in G minor (2 flats), what key signature does the clarinet in B♭ part show?
options: 2 flats (the same as strings — G minor)
No flats or sharps (0 — A minor, a tone higher)
gold.explanation: The clarinet in B♭ transposes up a tone. If the sounding key is G minor (2 flats), the clarinet part is written a tone higher — in A minor (0 flats). So the clarinet part has no flats in its key signature while the rest of the orchestra has 2 flats. This is the transposition: written in A minor to sound in G minor.

gold.question: In an orchestral score, how would you quickly identify which stave belongs to the viola (without reading the instrument label)?
options: The viola always has the same key signature as the clarinet.
The viola uses the alto clef (C clef on the middle line) — the only orchestral instrument that routinely does so.
The viola stave has a 'V' symbol instead of a clef.
The viola is always the loudest part and has the most notes per bar.
gold.explanation: The alto clef is the viola's signature: it is the only standard orchestral instrument that routinely uses it. If you see a C clef with the marker on the middle line of the staff, that is almost certainly the viola part. This is a reliable exam strategy — you do not need to read the label if you recognise the clef.

worked_examples.question: Looking at an orchestral score page, explain how you would identify which stave belongs to the viola, and what clef you would expect to find.
steps: Step 1 — score position. The viola is in the string section, which occupies the lowest staves of the score. Within the strings, the order is: first violins, second violins, violas, cellos, double basses. So the viola stave is third from the bottom of the string group.
Step 2 — alto clef. The viola is the only orchestral string that uses the alto clef (C clef on the middle line). This places middle C on the third line of the staff.

Step 3 — full answer. 'I would look in the string section (lower staves). The viola uses the alto clef — a C clef with the marker on the middle line. It is the only orchestral string to use this clef, so spotting an alto clef immediately identifies the viola part.'
